subject: chemistry
title: Naming organic compounds
summary: How to name and draw alkanes, alkenes, haloalkanes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, amines, amides and esters using IUPAC rules.
body:
Every organic compound has a systematic name that tells a chemist exactly how its atoms are joined, so anyone in the world can draw the same molecule from the name alone. The rules come from IUPAC (the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry). Being able to name and draw organic molecules is the foundation for everything else in Unit 4, from isomers to reaction pathways to analysing spectra.

## Think of it like this

### An IUPAC name is like a street address

A full address, such as unit number, street number, street name and suburb, lets anyone in Australia find exactly the same house. An IUPAC name does the same job for a molecule. The **parent chain** prefix (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-) is like the street, telling you how many carbons long it is. The numbers are like house numbers, showing where along the chain the **functional group** or branch sits, and the suffix (-ol, -al, -one, -oic acid) is like the type of building, telling you what lives there. Just as you number a street from one end so the house numbers are low and clear, you number the chain from the end that gives the main functional group the lowest number.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* streets are fixed on a map, but the "street" in a molecule is the longest continuous chain containing the functional group, and it may bend around corners in the way the molecule is drawn.

### A homologous series is like a set of train carriages

A **homologous series** is like a train where each version is one carriage longer than the last. Every train in the set has the same engine at the front (the same functional group, giving similar chemical properties), but each extra –CH₂– unit is another carriage. Longer trains are heavier and harder to move, just as longer molecules have stronger dispersion forces and higher boiling points, giving a gradual trend in physical properties.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* carriages can be added anywhere, but members of a homologous series also follow a general formula, such as CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ for alkanes, and branching changes the properties even when the number of carbons is the same.

### Ester names are like a band name with "featuring"

An ester is made from two parts, like a song by two artists. In the name, the alcohol part is said first and ends in **-yl** (ethyl), and the carboxylic acid part comes second and ends in **-oate** (ethanoate). The trick is that the semi-structural formula, such as CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, is often written acid part first, like a song listed under the other artist's name, so you have to work out which piece came from which "artist" before you name it.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* two artists choose the order of their names, but in IUPAC naming the order is fixed by the rule (alcohol part first), so there is only one correct name.

### In real life

Ingredient lists on food, cosmetics and medicines often include systematic or near-systematic names, such as ethanoic acid in vinegar or propan-2-ol in hand sanitiser and cleaning wipes. Many fruity smells and flavours are esters, and their names, like ethyl ethanoate, tell a chemist exactly which acid and alcohol they are made from.

## Key ideas

### Hydrocarbons, functional groups and homologous series

Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Carbon has four valence electrons, so it forms four covalent bonds. It can bond to other carbon atoms to make long chains, branched chains and rings.

A **hydrocarbon** is a compound made of only carbon and hydrogen. A **functional group** is an atom or group of atoms attached to the carbon chain that gives the molecule its typical chemical reactions. For example, the –OH group makes a molecule an alcohol and the –COOH group makes it a carboxylic acid.

A **homologous series** is a family of compounds that:

- have the same functional group
- share a general formula
- differ from the next member by one –CH₂– unit
- show similar chemical properties and a gradual trend in physical properties (for example, boiling point rises as the chain gets longer because dispersion forces get stronger)

| Series | Functional group | General formula | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alkanes | C–C single bonds only | CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ | propane, C₃H₈ |
| Alkenes | C=C double bond | CₙH₂ₙ | propene, C₃H₆ |
| Haloalkanes | –X (F, Cl, Br, I) | CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X | chloroethane, C₂H₅Cl |
| Alcohols | hydroxyl, –OH | CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH | ethanol, C₂H₅OH |
| Aldehydes | –CHO (C=O at chain end) | CₙH₂ₙ₊₁CHO | ethanal, CH₃CHO |
| Ketones | C=O within the chain | – | propanone, CH₃COCH₃ |
| Carboxylic acids | carboxyl, –COOH | CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH | ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH |
| Amines | amino, –NH₂ | CₙH₂ₙ₊₁NH₂ | methanamine, CH₃NH₂ |
| Amides | –CONH₂ (amide group) | – | ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂ |
| Esters | ester link, –COO– | – | methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃ |

Alkanes are **saturated** (only single C–C bonds). Alkenes are **unsaturated** because they contain a C=C double bond.

### Ways of drawing organic molecules

- A **molecular formula** shows only the number of each type of atom, e.g. C₂H₆O. It does not tell you the structure.
- A **structural formula** shows every atom and every bond as a line.
- A **semi-structural (condensed) formula** groups atoms around each carbon, e.g. CH₃CH₂OH for ethanol. Branches go in brackets: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃.
- A **skeletal formula** shows the carbon chain as a zigzag line. Each corner and each line end is a carbon atom. Hydrogens on carbon are not drawn; you add enough to give each carbon four bonds. All other atoms (O, N, Cl and the H atoms attached to them) are drawn in.

For example, the skeletal formula of butan-1-ol is a zigzag of four carbons with OH written at one end.

### The prefix tells you the chain length

| Carbons | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stem | meth- | eth- | prop- | but- | pent- | hex- | hept- | oct- |

### The general naming method

1. **Find the parent chain.** This is the longest continuous chain of carbons that contains the functional group (and the C=C bond for alkenes). It may bend; it does not have to be drawn in a straight line.
2. **Number the chain** from the end that gives the main functional group the lowest number. If there is a tie, give the branches (substituents) the lowest numbers.
3. **Name and locate branches.** Alkyl branches are methyl (–CH₃), ethyl (–C₂H₅) and so on. Halogens become prefixes: fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo. Use di-, tri-, tetra- when the same branch appears more than once, and list different branches in alphabetical order (ignore di-, tri- when alphabetising).
4. **Add the ending (suffix)** for the main functional group.
5. **Punctuate:** numbers are separated from each other by commas and from words by hyphens, e.g. 2,3-dimethylpentane.

### Endings for each functional group

| Group | Suffix or prefix | Example name | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alkane | -ane | 2-methylbutane | |
| Alkene | -ene | but-2-ene | number the first carbon of the C=C |
| Haloalkane | chloro-, bromo- etc. | 2-bromopropane | halogen is a prefix |
| Alcohol | -ol | propan-2-ol | number the carbon holding –OH |
| Aldehyde | -al | butanal | always C1, so no number needed |
| Ketone | -one | butan-2-one | C=O cannot be at the end |
| Carboxylic acid | -oic acid | propanoic acid | always C1, no number needed |
| Amine | -amine | ethanamine, propan-2-amine | |
| Amide | -amide | propanamide | always C1, no number needed |
| Ester | alkyl alkanoate | ethyl propanoate | two-word name |

The carbon of an aldehyde, carboxylic acid or amide group is counted as part of the parent chain. So CH₃CH₂COOH has three carbons and is propanoic acid, not ethanoic acid.

### Alcohols: primary, secondary and tertiary

Alcohols are classified by how many carbon atoms are bonded to the carbon carrying the –OH:

- **Primary (1°)**: that carbon is bonded to one other carbon (or none, as in methanol), e.g. propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.
- **Secondary (2°)**: bonded to two carbons, e.g. propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.
- **Tertiary (3°)**: bonded to three carbons, e.g. 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH.

This matters because each type behaves differently when oxidised (covered in the organic reactions lesson).

### Naming esters

An ester forms from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Its name has two words:

- The **first word** comes from the alcohol and ends in **-yl** (methyl, ethyl, propyl).
- The **second word** comes from the carboxylic acid and ends in **-oate** (methanoate, ethanoate, propanoate).

In the semi-structural formula CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, the part written with C=O (CH₃CO–) comes from the acid (ethanoic acid) and the part attached to the single-bonded O (–CH₂CH₃) comes from the alcohol (ethanol). So the name is ethyl ethanoate. Watch out: the formula is often written acid part first, but the name says the alcohol part first.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: a branched alcohol

Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂OH.

1. Longest chain containing the carbon with –OH: C(OH)–C–C(CH₃)–C. That is 4 carbons, so the stem is but-.
2. Number from the –OH end so the –OH is on C1. The methyl branch is then on C3.
3. Branch: 3-methyl.
4. Suffix: -ol on C1, so butan-1-ol.

**Name: 3-methylbutan-1-ol.** It is a primary alcohol because the C bearing –OH is attached to only one other carbon.

### Example 2: an ester from its formula

Name CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ and give the acid and alcohol it is made from.

1. Find the C=O carbon. The side containing it is CH₃CH₂CO–, which has 3 carbons, so it comes from propanoic acid and gives "propanoate".
2. The group on the single-bonded O is –CH₃, from methanol, which gives "methyl".
3. Alcohol part first: **methyl propanoate**, made from propanoic acid and methanol.

### Example 3: an alkene with a halogen

Name CH₂=CHCHClCH₃.

1. Chain of 4 carbons containing the C=C: but-.
2. Number from the left so the double bond starts at C1 (from the right it would start at C3). The Cl is then on C3.
3. **Name: 3-chlorobut-1-ene.**

### Example 4: reading a skeletal formula

A skeletal formula shows a zigzag of five corners and ends, with a C=O drawn at the second carbon.

1. Count carbons: 5, so pent-.
2. A C=O inside the chain is a ketone, -one.
3. Number so the C=O has the lowest number: C2.
4. **Name: pentan-2-one**, semi-structural formula CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃, molecular formula C₅H₁₀O.

## Common mistakes

- Picking the chain that is drawn straight instead of the longest continuous chain. Always trace every possible path.
- Forgetting that the carbon in –COOH, –CHO and –CONH₂ is part of the parent chain.
- Writing ester names backwards. The alcohol part (-yl) comes first even though the formula usually shows the acid part first.
- Numbering from the wrong end. The main functional group gets the lowest number first; branches only decide ties.
- Calling an alkyl branch on C1 a branch. A "methyl" on the end carbon just makes the chain longer (there is no 1-methylpropane; it is butane).

## Exam tips

- VCE questions often give a skeletal or semi-structural formula and ask for the IUPAC name, or give a name and ask you to draw the structure. Show all H atoms on O and N in skeletal formulas.
- Punctuation and spacing count: "propan-2-ol", not "2-propanol" or "propan 2 ol".
- When asked to draw a structural formula, show every bond, including the O–H bond.
- Use the VCE data book's functional group tables to check suffixes if you are unsure.

## Tips to remember

- **"Monkeys Eat Peeled Bananas"** — **Meth** (1), **Eth** (2), **Prop** (3), **But** (4). From five carbons on, the stems match the shapes: **pent**agon (5), **hex**agon (6), **hept**agon (7), **oct**opus (8).
- **Name it in four moves**: find the longest chain that holds the functional group (trace every path — it may bend), number from the end that gives the functional group the lowest number, add branches in alphabetical order, then add the ending.
- **"End-of-the-line groups don't need a number"**: aldehydes (-al), carboxylic acids (-oic acid) and amides (-amide) are always on C1, and their carbon counts in the chain. So CH₃CH₂COOH is **prop**anoic acid, not ethanoic acid.
- **Esters: "Alcohol says hi first"**: the name starts with the alcohol part (-yl) and ends with the acid part (-oate), even though the formula usually shows the acid part first. CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ = ethyl ethanoate.
- **1°, 2°, 3° alcohols — count the carbon "friends"**: the carbon holding –OH is bonded to one other carbon (primary), two (secondary) or three (tertiary).
- **Quick self-check**: if your name has "1-methyl" in it, your chain isn't the longest — a methyl on the end carbon just makes the chain longer (there is no 1-methylpropane; it is butane).

## Key terms

- **Hydrocarbon** — a compound containing only carbon and hydrogen.
- **Functional group** — an atom or group of atoms that gives an organic molecule its characteristic reactions.
- **Homologous series** — a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, each member differing by –CH₂–.
- **Saturated** — containing only single carbon–carbon bonds.
- **Unsaturated** — containing at least one carbon–carbon double (or triple) bond.
- **Parent chain** — the longest continuous carbon chain containing the main functional group.
- **Skeletal formula** — a drawing in which carbon atoms are line ends and corners and H atoms on carbon are left out.
- **Semi-structural formula** — a condensed formula showing which atoms are bonded to each carbon, e.g. CH₃CH₂OH.
- **Primary, secondary, tertiary alcohol** — the –OH carbon is bonded to one, two or three other carbons.

## Summary

- Organic molecules are named by finding the longest chain with the functional group, numbering it, naming the branches and adding the suffix.
- Chain length prefixes run meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-, hept-, oct-.
- Each homologous series has its own ending: -ane, -ene, -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, -amine, -amide, and esters are named alkyl alkanoate.
- Molecules can be shown as molecular, structural, semi-structural or skeletal formulas.
- Alcohols are primary, secondary or tertiary depending on how many carbons are attached to the –OH carbon.
- Members of a homologous series share chemical properties, while their boiling points rise as the chain gets longer.

questions.prompt: Which name is the correct IUPAC name for CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH?
questions.explanation: The –COOH carbon is counted in the parent chain, giving 4 carbons, so the name is butanoic acid. No number is needed because the carboxyl carbon is always C1. 'Propanoic acid' is the tempting wrong answer from forgetting to count the carboxyl carbon.

questions.prompt: What is the general formula of the alkene homologous series?
questions.explanation: An alkene with one C=C double bond has two fewer hydrogens than the alkane with the same number of carbons, giving CₙH₂ₙ (e.g. ethene, C₂H₄). CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ is the alkane formula, a common mix-up.

questions.prompt: What is the IUPAC name of the ester CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The part containing C=O, CH₃CO–, comes from ethanoic acid (ethanoate). The group on the single-bonded oxygen, –CH₂CH₂CH₃, comes from propan-1-ol (propyl). Alcohol part first gives propyl ethanoate. 'Ethyl propanoate' is the trap of reading the name in the order the formula is written.

questions.prompt: Which of these alcohols is a secondary alcohol?
questions.explanation: In butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, the carbon carrying –OH is bonded to two other carbons, so it is secondary. 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tempting because its –OH is on C2, but that carbon is bonded to three carbons, making it tertiary.

questions.prompt: Why does boiling point increase from methane to ethane to propane?

options.A: Each extra carbon adds a hydrogen bond between molecules.
options.B: Longer molecules have more electrons and larger surface contact, so dispersion forces are stronger.
options.C: Longer molecules have stronger covalent bonds that must be broken when boiling.
options.D: Longer molecules are more polar, so dipole–dipole forces increase.

questions.explanation: Alkanes are non-polar and are held together only by dispersion forces, which increase with more electrons and more contact between molecules. Option C is the most tempting misconception: boiling separates molecules and does not break covalent bonds within them.

questions.prompt: A skeletal formula shows a zigzag chain of 4 carbons with a C=O group on the second carbon. What is the compound?
questions.explanation: A C=O group inside the chain (not at the end) is a ketone. Four carbons with C=O at C2 is butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃. Butanal is tempting but in an aldehyde the C=O must be at the end of the chain (C1).

questions.prompt: What is the correct name for CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(Cl)CH₃?
questions.explanation: The chain has 4 carbons with a Cl and a methyl on neighbouring carbons. Both numbering directions give the set {2,3}, so the tie is broken alphabetically: chloro comes before methyl and gets the lower number. This gives 2-chloro-3-methylbutane. Option A uses the right numbers but gives the lower number to methyl; option B also lists the prefixes out of alphabetical order.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the members of a homologous series is correct?

options.A: They all have the same molecular formula.
options.B: They all have the same boiling point.
options.C: They differ from each other by one –CH₂– unit and have similar chemical reactions.
options.D: They contain different functional groups but the same number of carbons.

questions.explanation: A homologous series shares a functional group and general formula, with each member one –CH₂– longer than the last, so they react in similar ways. Option A describes isomers, not a homologous series, and option B is wrong because boiling points change gradually along the series.
